body.text:
ācāryadharmakīrtiviracitā sambandhaparīkṣā
(prabhācandrakṛtavyākhyopetā)
body.translated_text:
The <s>Sambandhaparīkṣā</s> (Examination of Relations) composed by <s>Ācārya Dharmakīrti</s>,
(with the commentary by <s>Prabhācandra</s>)

body.text: nanu cāṇū nāmayaḥśalākākalpatvenānyonyaṃ sambandhābhāvataḥ sthūlādipratīterbhrāntatvāt kathaṃ tadvaśāt tatsvabhāvo bhāvaḥ syāt? tathā hi - sambandho 'rthānāṃ pāratantryalakṣaṇo vā syāt, rūpaśleṣalakṣaṇo vā syāt? prathamapakṣe kimasau niṣpannayoḥ sambandhinoḥ syāt, aniṣpannayorvā? na tāvadaniṣpannayoḥ; svarūpasyaivāsattvāt śaśāśvaviṣāṇavat / niṣpannayośca pāratantryābhāvādasambandha eva /
body.translated_text: Now then, since atoms are like needle-tips in nature, and since there is no mutual relation among them, and since the perception of gross objects and the like is erroneous — how could an entity have that nature on account of that [relation]? For indeed, is relation (<s>sambandha</s>) among objects characterized by dependence (<s>pāratantrya</s>), or characterized by physical contact (<s>rūpaśleṣa</s>)? In the first case, does it apply to established relata, or to unestablished ones? Not to unestablished ones, certainly — because their very nature is non-existent, like the horns of a hare. And for established ones, since there is no dependence, there is simply no relation.

children.translated_text: And it has been said—

children.text: pāratantryaṃ hi sambandhaḥ siddhe kā paratantratā /
children.translated_text: For dependence is relation; when [an entity] is established, what dependence is there?

children.text: tasmāt sarvasya bhāvasya sambandho nāsti tattvataḥ // 1 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, for any entity whatsoever, there is no relation in reality. // 1 //

body.text:
nāpi rūpaśleṣalakṣaṇo 'sau; sambandhinordvitve rūpaśleṣavirodhāt /
tayoraikye vā sutarāṃ sambandhābhāvaḥ, sambandhinorabhāve sambandhāyogāt; dviṣṭhatvāttasya / atha nairantaryaṃ tayo rūpaśleṣaḥ? na; asyāntarālabhāvarūpatvenātāttvikatvāt sambandharūpatvāyogaḥ / nirantaratāyāśca sambandharūpatve sāntaratāpi kathaṃ sambandho na syāt?
body.translated_text: Nor is it characterized by physical contact; for if the relata are two, physical contact contradicts [their] duality. Or if they are one, there is even more so no relation, since in the absence of relata, relation is impossible — because it requires two bases. But then, is their contiguity (<s>nairantarya</s>) the physical contact? No, because since this has the nature of an intervening entity, it is not genuine, and hence cannot constitute a relation. And if non-separation were the nature of relation, how would separation also not be a relation?

body.text: kiñca- asau rūpaśleṣaḥ sarvātmanā, ekadeśena vā syāt? sarvātmanā rūpaśleṣe aṇūnāṃ piṇḍaḥ aṇumātraḥ syāt / ekadeśena tacchaleṣe kimekadeśāstasyātmabhūtāḥ, parabhūtā vā? ātmabhūtāścet; na ekadeśena rūpaśleṣastadabhāvāt / parabhūtāścet; tairapyaṇūnāṃ sarvātmanaikadeśena vā rūpaśleṣe sa eva paryanuyogaḥ, anavasthā ca syāt / taduktam-
body.translated_text: Moreover — is this physical contact total or partial? If total physical contact, the aggregate of atoms would be merely atom-sized. If partial contact with it, are those parts intrinsic to it, or extrinsic? If intrinsic — there is no partial physical contact, because of the absence of [distinct] parts. If extrinsic — then the same objection applies regarding the atoms' total or partial contact with those [parts], and there would be infinite regress. Thus it has been said—

children.text: rūpaśleṣo hi sambadho dvitve sa ca kathaṃ bhavet /
children.translated_text: For physical contact is relation, but how can it exist when there is duality?
Therefore, for entities that are intrinsically different, there is no relation in reality. // 2 //

body.text: kiñca- parāpakṣaiva sambandhaḥ, tasya dviṣṭhatvāt / taṃ cāpekṣate bhāvaḥ svayaṃ san, asan vā? na tāvadasan; apekṣādharmāśrayatvavirodhāt kharaśṛṅgavat / nāpi san; sarvanirāśaṃsatvāt, anyathā sattvavirodhāt / tanna parāpekṣā nāma yadrūpaḥ sambandhaḥ siddhyet /
body.translated_text: Moreover — relation is indeed dependence on another (<s>parāpekṣā</s>), since it requires two bases. Does an entity depend on another when it itself is existent, or non-existent? Not when non-existent, certainly — because this contradicts being a substratum of the property of dependence, like a hare's horn. Nor when existent — because [an existent entity] expects nothing whatsoever; otherwise, its very existence would be contradicted. Therefore, there is nothing called 'dependence on another' such that relation could be established.

children.translated_text: And it has been said—
For dependence on another is relation; how can what is non-existent depend?
And an existent entity, expecting nothing at all — how can it depend? // 3 //

body.text: kiñca- asau sambandhaḥ sambandhibhyāṃ bhinnaḥ, abhinno vā? yadyabhinnaḥ; tadā sambandhināveva, na sambandhaḥ kaścit, sa eva vā, na tāviti? bhinnaścet; sambandhinau kevalau kathaṃ sambaddhau syātām?
body.translated_text: Moreover — is this relation different from, or identical with, the relata? If identical, then there are only the relata and no relation whatsoever; or if the relation is identical [with one], then it does not exist in the other. If different, how would the bare relata be connected?

body.text: bhavatu vā sambandho 'rthāntaram; tathāpi tenaikena sambandhena saha dvayoḥ sambandhinoḥ kaḥ sambandhaḥ? yathā sambandhinoryathoktadoṣānna kaścit sambandhaḥ, tathātrāpi / tenānayoḥ sambandhāntarābhyupagame cānavasthā syāt; tatrāpi sambandhāntarānuṣaṅgāt / tanna sambandhinoḥ sambandhabuddhirvāstavī; tavadyatirekeṇānyasya sambandhasyāsambhavāt / taduktam-
body.translated_text: Or, granted that relation is a separate entity; still, what is the relation of the two relata with that one relation? Just as, for the reasons stated, there is no relation between the relata, the same applies here. And if yet another relation between them is postulated, there would be infinite regress — since yet another relation would be entailed there too. Therefore, the cognition of relation between relata is not real, since apart from them no other relation is possible. Thus it has been said—

children.translated_text: If relation exists because of connecting the two with one, then of those two,
what relation is there? And there would be infinite regress; thus the notion of relation [is not real]. // 4 //
Therefore—

children.text: tau ca bhāvau tadanyaśca sarve te svātmani sthitāḥ /
children.translated_text: Those two entities, and what is other than them — all abide in their own nature.
Thus entities are unmixed in themselves; conceptual construction (<s>kalpanā</s>) mixes them. // 5 //

body.text: tau ca bhāvau sambandhinau tābhyāmanyaśca sambandhaḥ, sarve te svātmani svasvarūpe sthitāḥ / tenāmiśrā vyāvṛttasvarūpāḥ svayaṃ bhāvāḥ, tathāpi tānmiśrayati yojayati kalpanā // 5 //
body.translated_text: Those two entities — the relata — and what is other than them — namely the relation — all abide in their own nature, in their own form. Therefore, entities are unmixed, having distinct natures, in themselves; yet conceptual construction (<s>kalpanā</s>) mixes, that is, conjoins them. // 5 //

body.text: ata eva tadvāstavasambandhābhāve 'pi tāmeva kalpanāmanurundhānairvyavahartṛbhirbhāvānāṃ bhedo 'nyāpohaḥ, tasya pratyāyanāya kriyākārakādivācinaḥ śabdāḥ prayojyante- 'devadatta gāmabhyāja śuklāṃ daṇḍena ityādayaḥ / na khalu kārakāṇāṃ kriyayā sambandho 'sti; kṣaṇikatvena kriyākāle kārakāṇāmasambhavāt / uktañca-
body.translated_text: Therefore, even in the absence of their real relation, those who engage in practical affairs, following that very conceptual construction, [understand] the differentiation of entities as <s>anyāpoha</s> (exclusion of the other). For conveying that, words expressing action, agent, and so forth are employed — '<s>Devadatta</s>, drive the white cow with a stick,' and so on. Indeed there is no real relation of the <s>kārakas</s> (grammatical agents) with the action, since due to momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikatva</s>), the <s>kārakas</s> do not exist at the time of the action. And it has been said—

children.translated_text: And by those who conform to that [convention], words denoting action and agent
are combined as designators for the purpose of conveying distinctions of entities. // 6 //
Even the relation of cause and effect (<s>kāryakāraṇabhāva</s>), since the two do not co-exist,
how can it be established? How can there be a relation in what abides in two [separate loci] when it does not abide in two? // 7 //

body.text: kāryakāraṇabhāvastarhi sambadho bhaviṣyati- ityapyasamīcīnam, kāryakāraṇayorasahabhāvatastasyāpi dviṣṭhasyāsambhavāt / na khalu kāraṇakāle kāryaṃ tatkāle vā kāraṇamasti, tulyakālaṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvanupapatteḥ, savyetaragoviṣāṇavat / tanna sambandhinau sahabhāvinau vidyete yeṃnānayorvartamāno 'sau sambandhaḥ syāt / adviṣṭhe ca bhāve sambandhatānupapannaiva // 7 //
body.translated_text: [Objection:] 'Then the relation of cause and effect will constitute the connection.' This too is incorrect, because due to the non-co-existence of cause and effect, even that [relation], which would abide in two [loci], is impossible. For indeed, the effect does not exist at the time of the cause, nor does the cause [exist] at the time of [the effect]; a simultaneous relation of cause and effect is untenable — like the left and right horns of a cow. Therefore, there do not exist two relata that co-exist, in which that relation, being present, could subsist. And a relation in a non-dual locus is simply untenable. // 7 //

children.translated_text: Existing sequentially in one [locus alone], independent of the other,
[the relation] exists even in its [the other's] absence because of [its] existence in that [one alone]; therefore the relation does not abide in one [thing only]. // 8 //

body.text: kārye kāraṇe vā krameṇāsau sambandho vartate- ityapyasāmpratam; yataḥ krameṇāpi bhāvaḥ sambandhākhya ekatra kāraṇe kārye vā varttamāno 'nyanispṛhaḥ kāryakāraṇayoranyatarānapekṣo naikavṛttimān sambandho yuktaḥ; tadabhāvepi kāryakāraṇayorabhāve 'pi tadbhāvāt // 8 //
body.translated_text: [Objection:] 'That relation subsists sequentially in the effect or in the cause.' This too is incorrect; for a real entity called 'relation,' existing sequentially in one [locus] — either the cause or the effect — and independent of the other, not requiring either of the cause or the effect, is not tenable as a relation that abides in a single [thing]; because it would exist even in the absence of that — even in the absence of the cause or the effect. // 8 //

children.translated_text: If, depending on one of the two, it operates in the other,
then what is depended upon must be a helper — but how can what is non-existent help? // 9 //

body.text: yadi punaḥ kāryakāraṇayorekaṃ kāryaṃ kāraṇaṃ vāpekṣyānyatra kārye kāraṇe vāsau sambandhaḥ krameṇa varttata iti saspṛhatvena dviṣṭha eveṣyate; tadānenāpekṣyamāṇenopakāriṇā bhavitavyam, yasmādupakāryapekṣyaḥ syāt, nānyaḥ / kathaṃ copakarotyasan? yadā kāraṇakāle kāryākhyo bhāvo 'san tatkāle vā kāraṇākhyastadā naivopakuryād; asāmarthyāt // 9 //
body.translated_text: [Objection:] 'If, depending on one of the two — cause or effect — that relation operates sequentially in the other — effect or cause — then it is accepted as abiding in two, precisely because it is dependent.' [Reply:] In that case, what is depended upon must be a helper, since it is the helper that is to be depended upon, not anything else. But how can what is non-existent help? When at the time of the cause the entity called 'effect' is non-existent, or at its [the effect's] time the entity called 'cause' [is non-existent], then it could not help at all — because of incapacity. // 9 //

children.translated_text: If the relation of cause and effect between the two is established from connection with a single object,
then from the connection of duality [number] and so forth, [it would follow] for the left and right horns [of a cow] as well. // 10 //

body.text: kiñca- yadyekārthābhisambandhāt kāryakāraṇatā tayoḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvatvenābhimatayoḥ; tarhi dvitvasaṃkhyāparatvāparatvavibhāgādisambandhāt prāptā sā savyetaragoviṣāṇayorapi // 10 //
body.translated_text: Moreover — if the relation of cause and effect between those two regarded as being in a cause-effect relation is [established] from connection with a single object, then from the connection of duality-number, otherness, posteriority, and separation, that [causal relation] would follow for the left and right horns of a cow as well. // 10 //

children.text: dviṣṭho hi kaścit sambandho nāto 'nyattasya lakṣaṇam /
children.translated_text: A relation is [by definition] something that abides in two [loci]; therefore there is no other defining characteristic of it.
If the condition for the connection is the existence-and-absence of one upon [the existence-and-absence of] the other — that is the relation of cause and effect. // 11 //

body.text: na yena kenacidekena sambandhāt seṣyate; kiṃ tarhi? sambandhalakṣaṇenaiveti cet; tanna, dviṣṭho hi kaścitpadārthaḥ sambandhaḥ, nāto 'rthadvayābhisambandhādanyat tasya lakṣaṇam, yenāsya saṃkhyāderviśeṣo vyavasthāpyeta // 11 //
body.translated_text: [Objection:] It is not established by just any single connection. Rather, [it is established] by the very defining characteristic of relation. [Reply:] That is not so, for a relation is a real entity that abides in two [loci]; there is no other defining characteristic of it besides the connection with two objects, by which its distinction from number and the like could be established. // 11 //

children.translated_text: The condition for the connection is not those very [things] themselves. What then is the relation of cause and effect here?
If [you say it is] because of a difference — but this word [i.e., 'cause and effect'] depends on a stipulator. // 12 //

body.text: kasyacidbhāve bhāvo 'bhāve cābhāvaḥ, tāvupādhī viśeṣaṇaṃ yasya yogasya=sambandhasya sa kāryakāraṇatā yadi na sarvasambandhaḥ; tadā tāveva yogopādhī bhāvābhāvau kāryakāraṇatāstu, kimasatsambandhakalpanayā? bhedāccet 'bhāve hi bhāvo 'bhāve cābhāvaḥ' iti bahavo 'bhidheyāḥ kathaṃ kāryakāraṇatetyekārthābhidhāyinā śabdenocyante? nanvayaṃ śabdo niyoktāraṃ samāśritaḥ / niyoktā hi yaṃ śabdaṃ yathā prayuṅkte tathā prāha, ityanekatrāpyekā śrutirna virudhyate iti tāveva kāryakāraṇatā // 12 //
body.translated_text: The existence of one upon the existence [of the other] and the absence [of one] upon the absence [of the other] — if these two are the qualifying conditions (<s>upādhi</s>) of that connection, [and] that is the relation of cause and effect, then [it is] not every relation [that is causal]. In that case, those very qualifying conditions of the connection — existence and absence — are themselves the relation of cause and effect; what need is there for imagining a non-existent 'relation'? If [you say] 'because of a difference' — [namely that] 'existence upon existence and absence upon absence' designates many things, how can they be denoted by the single word 'cause-and-effect'? But this word depends on a stipulator. For a stipulator employs a word in whatever way he wishes, and thus a single utterance even for multiple things is not contradictory — therefore those very [conditions of co-presence and co-absence] are the relation of cause and effect. // 12 //

children.translated_text: One who sees one [thing] — when seeing and not-seeing what was previously unseen —
even without explicators, a person follows the effect when he does not see [the cause]. // 13 //

body.text: yasmāt paśyannekaṃ kāraṇābhimatamupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasyādṛṣṭasya kāryākhyasya darśane sati tadadarśane ca satyapaśyatkāryamanveti 'idamato bhavati' iti pratipadyate janaḥ 'ata idaṃ jātam' ityākhyātṛbhirvināpi // 13 //
body.translated_text: Because one who sees one [thing] — [namely] what is regarded as the cause, when there is the seeing of something previously unseen (i.e., whose criterion of perception is now met) — [that is,] the [thing] called 'effect,' and when there is the not-seeing of that [effect], one who does not see [it] follows the effect — [thinks] 'this arises from that' — a person understands [thus] even without explicators [telling him] 'this was born from that.' // 13 //

children.translated_text: Since the cognition of an effect is impossible apart from seeing and not-seeing,
the verbal designation 'effect' and so forth is employed here just for the sake of brevity. // 14 //

body.text: tasmād darśanādarśane viṣayiṇi viṣayopacārāt- bhāvābhāvau muktvā kāryabuddherasambhavāt kāryādiśrutirapyatra 'bhāvābhāvayormā lokaḥ pratipadamiyatīṃ śabdamālāmabhidadhyāt' iti vyavahāralāghavārthaṃ niveśiteti // 14 //
body.translated_text: Therefore, since seeing and non-seeing pertain to the subject [of cognition], and since, setting aside existence and non-existence as figurative extensions upon the object, the arising of an effect-cognition is impossible [without them], the scriptural usage of 'effect' and so forth is introduced here merely for the sake of convenience in conventional discourse, as [the author says]: 'Let not the world, at every step, employ such a string of words as "existence and non-existence."'

children.translated_text: The understanding of something as an effect of that [cause], which is described [in ordinary usage], arises from the presence and absence of that [cause];
That [understanding] is a designation pertaining to the domain of convention (<s>saṅketa</s>), just as the understanding of 'cow' [arises] from the dewlap and so forth.

body.text: anvayavyatirekābhyāṃ kāryakāraṇatā nānyā cet kathaṃ bhāvābhāvābhyāṃ sā prasādhyate? tadabhāvābhāvāt liṅgāt tatkāryatāgatiryāpyanuvarṇyate- 'asyedaṃ kāryaṃ kāraṇaṃ ca' iti; saṅketaviṣayākhyā sā / yathā 'gaurayaṃ sāsnādimattvāt' ityanena govyavahārasya viṣayaḥ pradarśyate // 15 //
body.translated_text: If causality (<s>kāryakāraṇatā</s>) is nothing other than [what is established through] positive correlation (<s>anvaya</s>) and negative correlation (<s>vyatireka</s>), how is it established through presence and absence? The understanding of something as an effect, [expressed as] 'this is its effect and that is its cause,' is described based on the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) of the absence of that [effect] when that [cause] is absent; that [understanding] is a designation pertaining to the domain of convention. Just as by [saying] 'this is a cow because it possesses a dewlap and so forth,' the object of the conventional usage of 'cow' is indicated.

children.text: bhāve bhāvini tadbhāvo bhāva eva ca bhāvitā /
children.translated_text: When the existent [cause] exists, the existence of that [effect follows]; and when [that cause] exists, there is the production [of the effect];
The cause-and-effect relationship is established through direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) and non-apprehension (<s>anupalambha</s>).

body.text: yataśca 'bhāve bhāvini=bhavanadharmiṇi tadbhāvaḥ=kāraṇābhimatasya bhāva eva kāraṇatvam, bhāve eva kāraṇābhimatasya bhāvitā kāryābhimatasya kāryatvam' iti prasiddhe pratyakṣānupalambhato hetuphalate / tato bhāvābhāvāveva kāryakāraṇatā, nānyā // 16 //
body.translated_text: Since 'when the existent [cause] exists' — that is, when the entity that possesses the property of coming-into-being [exists] — 'the existence of that' — that is, the existence of what is regarded as the cause, constitutes its causality; 'when [that cause] exists, the production' — that is, the effecthood of what is regarded as the effect — is established through direct perception and non-apprehension as the cause-and-effect relationship. Therefore, existence and non-existence alone constitute causality, and nothing else.

children.translated_text: Conceptual constructions (<s>vikalpa</s>s) whose objects have their true nature consisting in just this much, pertaining to the domain of cause and effect,
present [their] objects as if connected, [though they are] false in their [representation of] objects.

body.text: tenaitāvanmātraṃ=bhāvābhāvau tāveva tattvaṃ 'yasyārthasyāsāvetāvanmātratattvaḥ, so 'rtho yeṣāṃ vikalpānāṃ te etāvanmātratattvārthāḥ=etāvanmātrabījāḥ kāryakāraṇagocarāḥ, darśayanti ghaṭitāniva=sambaddhānivāsambaddhānapyarthān / evaṃ ghaṭanācca mithyārthāḥ // 17 //
body.translated_text: Therefore, 'just this much' — namely, existence and non-existence — that alone is the true nature. 'Whose objects have their true nature consisting in just this much' means: those conceptual constructions for which this object has a true nature of just this much — they are 'having just-this-much as their true nature of objects,' i.e., having just this much as their basis, pertaining to the domain of cause and effect, and they present objects that are unconnected as if connected. And because of [this false] connecting, they are 'false in their objects.'

children.translated_text: If [things are] distinct, what connection [can there be]? And if [they are] non-distinct, what causality [can there be]?

children.text: bhāvehyanyasya viśliṣṭau śliṣṭau syātāṃ kathaṃ ca tau // 18 //
children.translated_text: For when one [thing] exists, how could the two — [being] separate — be joined?

body.text: kiñca, asau kāryakāraṇabhūto 'rtho bhinnaḥ, abhinno vā syāt? yadi bhinnaḥ;, tarhi bhinne kā ghaṭanā svasvabhāvavyavasthiteḥ? athābhinnaḥ; tadābhinne kāryakāraṇatāpi kā? naiva syāt /
body.translated_text: Moreover, is the object that constitutes cause and effect distinct or non-distinct? If distinct, then what connection [can there be] between distinct [things], since each is established in its own nature? But if non-distinct, then what causality can there be in the case of non-distinct [things]? There would be none at all.

body.text: syādetat, na bhinnasyābhinnasya vā sambandhaḥ / kiṃ tarhi? sambandhākhyenaikena sambandhāt; ityatrāpi bhāve sattāyāmanyasya sambandhasya viśliṣṭau kāryakāraṇābhimatau śliṣṭau syātām, kathaṃ ca tau saṃyogisamavāyinau? ādigrahaṇāt svasvāmyādikam // 18 //
body.translated_text: One might say: it is not the case that there is a relation of the distinct or the non-distinct. What then? [There is a relation] through a single [entity] called 'relation.' In that case too, when that other relation exists, how could those two — the supposed cause and effect, [being] separate — become joined? And how could those two be of the nature of conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) and inherence (<s>samavāya</s>)? By the word 'etc.' [in the verse], the owner-property relation and similar [relations are also included].

children.translated_text: Conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), inherence (<s>samavāya</s>), and so forth — all of this has been examined by the foregoing [argument];
And because of mutual non-contribution, such a relatum (<s>sambandhī</s>) does not [exist].

body.text: sarvametenāntantaroktena sāmānyasambandhapratiṣedhena cintitam saṃyogyādīnāmanyonyamanupakārāccājanyajanakabhāvācca na sambandhī ca tādṛśo 'nupakāryopakārakabhūtaḥ // 19 //
body.translated_text: All of this — [namely] conjunction and so forth — has been examined by the general refutation of relations stated above; and because of mutual non-contribution — that is, because of the absence of the relationship of producer and produced — such a relatum, one that would be the beneficiary and the benefactor, does not [exist].

children.translated_text: For even in the production of an effect by something that is inherent (<s>samavāyin</s>),
that [thing] is not inherent at that time [of production]; therefore [the argument leads to] overextension (<s>atiprasaṅga</s>).

body.text: athāsti kaścit samavāyī yo 'vayavirūpaṃ kāryaṃ janayati, ato nānupakārādasambandhiteti; tanna; yato janane 'pi kāryasya kenacit samavāyinābhyupagamyamāne samavāyī, nāsau tadā; jananakāle kāryasyāniṣpatteḥ / na ca tato jananāt samavāyitvaṃ siddhyati; kumbhakārāderapi ghaṭe samavāyitvaprasaṅgāt // 20 //
body.translated_text: But suppose there is some inherent [entity] that produces an effect in the form of a part-whole [configuration]; therefore, it is not the case that there is no relation due to non-contribution — [if so,] that is wrong. For even when the production of an effect by some inherent [entity] is admitted, that [entity] is not inherent at the time [of production], since the effect has not yet come into being at the time of production. Nor is inherence established merely from that production, since there would be the overextension of even a potter and the like being inherent in a pot.

children.translated_text: Even when those two [are] mutually non-contributing, if there is a relation through inherence or elsewhere,

children.text: sambandho yadi viśvaṃ syāt samavāyi parasparam // 21 //
children.translated_text: then the entire [universe] would be mutually inherent.

body.text: tayoḥ samavāyinoḥ parasparamanupakāre 'pi tābhyāṃ vā samavāyasya nityatayā samavāyena vā tayoḥ paratra vā kvacidanupakāre 'pi sambandho yadīṣyate; tadā viśvaṃ parasparāsambaddhaṃ samavāyi parasparaṃ syāt // 21 //
body.translated_text: Even when those two inherent [entities] are mutually non-contributing, if a relation is accepted between them — or [between them and] inherence, which is eternal — or through inherence, or elsewhere, even in [cases of] non-contribution, then the entire [universe], [being equally] unconnected with one another, would be mutually inherent.

children.translated_text: Even if [you hold that] conjunction is produced [and therefore relates the two], those two are not then conjoined [at the time of production];
because the absurd consequence of [everything] being connected with action and so forth [would follow]; and persistence [of conjunction] has [already] been refuted.

body.text: ityācāryadharmakīrtiviracitā sambandhaparīkṣā samāptā /
body.translated_text: Thus the <s>Sambandhaparīkṣā</s> (Examination of Relations), composed by the master <s>Dharmakīrti</s>, is concluded.

body.text: yadi ca saṃyogasya kāryatvāttasya tābhyāṃ jananāt saṃyogitā tayoḥ tadā saṃyogajanane 'piṣṭau, tataḥ saṃyogajananānna tau saṃyoginau, karmaṇo 'pi saṃyogitāpatteḥ / saṃyogo hyanyatarakarmajaḥ ubhayakarmajaśceṣyate / ādigrahaṇāt saṃyogasyāpi saṃyogitā syāt / na saṃyogajananāt saṃyogitā, kintarhi? sthāpanāditi cet; na sthitiśca prativarṇitā=granthāntare pratikṣiptā, sthāpyasthāpakayorjanyajanakatvābhāvānnānyā sthitiriti // 22 //
body.translated_text: And if, because conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) is an effect and is produced by those two [substances], the state of being conjoined (<s>saṃyogitā</s>) belongs to those two, then even in the production of conjunction [the same reasoning] is desired. Therefore, from the production of conjunction, those two are not [truly] conjoined — because the state of being conjoined would also apply to action (<s>karman</s>). For conjunction is accepted as produced either from the action of one [substance] or from the actions of both. Because of the word 'and so forth' (<s>ādigrahaṇa</s>), even conjunction itself would have the state of being conjoined. If [one says that] the state of being conjoined does not arise from the production of conjunction, but rather from 'maintenance' (<s>sthāpana</s>) — [we reply:] no, for persistence (<s>sthiti</s>) has been refuted — [it was] rejected in another treatise — because there is no relation of produced and producer between what is maintained and the maintainer, there is no other 'persistence.' (22)

body.text: iti prabhācandrakṛtā sambandhaparīkṣāvyākhyā samāptā /
body.translated_text: Thus ends the commentary on the <s>Saṃbandhaparīkṣā</s> (Examination of Relations), composed by <s>Prabhācandra</s>.
